baseline.text: This movement originated in the Western Qin Great Revolution of 1810. People of this age viewed it as a modern economic transformation arising within agrarian eastern societies rooted in clan structures. Its method was to confiscate or redeem over-concentrated land from old owners and redistribute it among peasants, thereby freeing resources to the market. In politics, the reforms aim to grab power from old military nobles by physically reduce their wealth and means to control their 'clansmen'. As Northern Ming nobilities, with their highly militarised tradition in local ruling, are widely regarded as the source of chaos and poverty among the people of the old northern regimes. The Chinese imperial ruling bloc once suspended this transformation during its rise. But around Mu Zhongtang's 1820 southern campaign, to revive the economy, liberate production, and mobilize peasants and soldiers from the bottom, Mu and his confidants reopened the movement.

The ruling bloc of the Empire of China was born in the great revolutionary era barely twenty years ago. They witnessed the old military clans and their two empires ground into dust by that vast upheaval. On those ruins, new officer corps led by Mu Zhongtang rose in the people's name, cleared out corruption and radical terror. Then, he the great led the founding of our great empire upon the promise of 'equal land rights and people's governance'.

Everything should have remained so...

At this moment of peril, the founding emperor decisively revived the slogan of 'land rights revolution'. Land reorganization profits and population mobility stabilized a faltering imperial economy. But as peace endured and reforms deepened, a dark current gathered in the shadows. Vested interests in the army, the tycoons, the officials, and even old gentry stripped of surplus lands began to return. Their schemes, resentment, and desire now corrode the foundations of the imperial ideals like some deadly acid...

candidate.text: In 1852, Mu Zhongtang, founding emperor of the Chinese Empire, died at the Menghua detached palace outside Bianliang. He was seventy years old and posthumously honored as Gao Emperor of Hua. As one of the most successful military commanders, statesmen, and strategists in Northern Ming China, Mu built a nationalist theoretical framework of lasting influence. Applying those theories, he founded a vast empire across North China, the Northeast, and Mongolia, greatly advanced Eastern industrial modernization, and to some extent inherited and preserved the legacy of the early-19th-century Western Qin Revolution.\n\nBefore his death, Mu foresaw inner-palace struggles among princes and unrest among old intimates such as Su Hong. He entrusted his younger sister Mu Muzi to veteran general Fei Xiyi and urged her to avoid political conflict as much as possible.

candidate.text:
Mu Muzi, younger sister of Mu Zhongtang, was nearly twenty years younger than her brother. Bright and dignified, she held steadfast loyalty. In Mu's later years she was uniquely favored: above all palace women, and often acting in his place to inspect armies and aid civilians when old Xiangyang wounds limited his mobility. Mu even assigned his capital-camp general Fei Xiyi to escort her, giving the princess great prestige. After Mu's death, she stepped forward to stabilize state affairs and stood among the foremost contributors to succession order.

Yet for the emperor's aunt to hold such authority over palace stability and military-civil peace inevitably reminded powerful old courtiers of Princess Taiping's precedent. In addition, many civil officials in the East Garden outside Bianliang - some nurturing more republican ideals - placed hopes in this populist noblewoman. Ultimately, veteran military elders of the Privy Council agreed to remove her and other unstable elements from decision-making by a 'gentle' method.

Thus, under the 'example' of retiring imperial marshal Fei Xiyi, a group of former capital-camp elders 'escorted' Mu Muzi to reside in the Eastern Continent as a long-term 'traveler.' She never returned to Mu Hua rule again.

candidate.text: Chronicles of the Northern Ming Warring States is a late-life novel by Mu Muzi, younger sister of founder Mu Zhongtang, written after the Chinese Great Revolution in the Northern Ming world. The work spans five major and ten minor volumes, 480 chapters, and nearly two million characters, with a composition period of thirty-five years. Mu Muzi departed from chaptered-serial conventions and rigid portrayals of princes and generals, drawing on the narrative strengths of classics such as Water Margin, Strange Tales, and Journey to the West to shape characters from every class and stratum of society. In a near-modern historical style, the book recounts over four centuries from the sudden death of Yongle in a 1408 hunt to the 1835 Treaty of Yangzhou and the north-south river partition. Because the work 'bears history's weight while transforming it with the spirit of fiction,' and 'tells both Chinese heroism and old-age suffering,' and is 'required reading for anyone seeking the roots of Asian modernity,' later generations ranked it among the Five Great Chinese Classics and one of the longest novels in human history.

随着旧宗族和土地不再能锁住农民，无数稚嫩、满是灰土却充满朝气的脸孔源源不断地从郊野涌入城市。他们憧憬新的生活。一种用人类的智慧和科学力量构建的生活。许多血缘的余孽用各种各样的地方团体伪装自己，试图重新夺回对这些人的控制。但巡捕的警棍和判官的惊堂木终会粉碎他们的野心。

baseline.text:
Our improved land code, labor code, and family-law civil clauses have now reached every corner of the empire, establishing a new economic order. In this order, people once bound for millennia by blood-clan structures have been liberated. The elevated ridges of private estate return to their character as natural resources.

As old clan and land bonds can no longer lock peasants in place, endless streams of young, dust-covered but vigorous faces pour from the countryside into the cities. They yearn for a new life built through human intelligence and scientific power. Remnants of bloodline privilege disguise themselves in local associations to reclaim control, but police batons and the magistrate's gavel will shatter their ambition.

Once again we have brought founder Mu Zhongtang's ideal into reality. We have proven this empire was built for the interests of the Huaxia nation. For that reason, it will protect even the smallest and most helpless person's freedom to choose their own fate - now pursued in the cities, where it creates new prosperity for the empire.
